extract:
Counting Crows formed in the San Francisco Bay Area in 1991, emerging from the Berkeley and San Francisco club circuit and remaining active ever since. The band grew out of a partnership between singer and songwriter Adam Duritz and guitarist David Bryson, who began performing as an acoustic duo before expanding into a full group. Early members included keyboardist Charlie Gillingham, bassist Matt Malley and drummer Steve Bowman. The band took its name from a line in a traditional counting rhyme about magpies, which equates their number with sorrow or joy.

Musically, the band drew openly on Van Morrison, The Band and R.E.M., blending folk-rock warmth with Duritz's confessional, densely detailed lyrics. Signed to DGC, a Geffen imprint, they recorded their debut, August and Everything After (1993), with producer T Bone Burnett. The album broke big on the strength of "Mr. Jones," a wry meditation on fame and longing, followed by the singles "Rain King" and "Omaha," while the sprawling "Round Here" became a fan touchstone. A high-profile appearance on Saturday Night Live helped propel the record to multi-platinum sales. That same era, the band performed Van Morrison's "Caravan" with Robbie Robertson when Morrison was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, underscoring their roots-rock lineage. Guitarist Dan Vickrey joined during this period, and drummer Ben Mize replaced Bowman.

Recovering the Satellites (1996), produced by Gil Norton, was a louder, more anxious record that grappled with sudden celebrity. It entered the Billboard 200 at number one and yielded "Angels of the Silences," the piano ballad "A Long December," and "Daylight Fading." The live set Across a Wire: Live in New York City followed in 1998. This Desert Life (1999), co-produced by David Lowery and Dennis Herring, struck a looser, sunnier tone, led by the upbeat "Hanginaround." Hard Candy (2002), produced by Steve Lillywhite, brought polished pop-rock with "American Girls," featuring backing vocals from Sheryl Crow. The album's cover of Joni Mitchell's "Big Yellow Taxi," featuring Vanessa Carlton, became a radio hit.

The band's widest exposure came with "Accidentally in Love," written for the Shrek 2 soundtrack in 2004, which earned an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song. Situated alongside the mid-1990s wave of melodic, roots-conscious rock acts that followed grunge, Counting Crows were sometimes grouped with post-grunge and adult-alternative radio. Their narrative songwriting and Duritz's emotive delivery, however, set them apart and drew both devoted fans and skeptics who found the earnestness overwrought. Duritz later spoke publicly about living with a dissociative disorder, adding context to the alienation running through many of his lyrics.

After Saturday Nights and Sunday Mornings (2008), the band left Geffen. They issued the covers album Underwater Sunshine (2012) independently, then released Somewhere Under Wonderland (2014). The four-song Butter Miracle, Suite One (2021) marked a return to ambitious, interconnected songwriting. Counting Crows continue to tour extensively, and their debut remains a defining document of 1990s American rock.
title: Counting Crows
